request: Hi, I'm doing Paper 2 Topic 10 (authoritarian states) and my case study is Mao's China. In my last practice essay on the Great Leap Forward I basically wrote "millions died because of Mao's bad policies" and got 6/15 - the comment was "no specific evidence, no awareness of debate". Can you explain what actually caused the famine during the Great Leap Forward (1958-62) and how bad it was, but with proper specifics I can use: dates, grain output figures, the actual policies (communes, backyard furnaces, the farming methods etc), named events like the conference where Mao's critic got purged, and the 1962 meeting where someone said it was mostly man-made (who said it?). Most importantly I need the different death toll estimates and WHO gives each one, because I want to write "according to X" instead of just "millions". Also where do historians actually disagree about whose fault it was - Mao personally, the system, local cadres, the weather? Please flag anything that's contested rather than giving me one number as if it's settled. I'm SL so this is for a 15 mark essay.
strong_answer_must: Date the Great Leap Forward precisely: launched 1958 under the Second Five-Year Plan; people's communes generalised after the Beidaihe Politburo resolution of August 1958 (roughly 26,000 communes covering about 99% of rural households by the end of 1958); backyard steel furnaces in autumn 1958 with the steel target doubled to 10.7 million tonnes; retreat and partial decollectivisation 1960-62.

Name the Lushan Conference (July-August 1959) as the event where Defence Minister Peng Dehuai criticised the Leap in a private letter to Mao (14 July 1959), was denounced as leader of an 'anti-Party clique', and was replaced by Lin Biao; explain that the ensuing anti-rightist drive silenced criticism and deepened the famine in 1959-60.

Identify the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference (January-February 1962) and attribute the judgement that the disaster was 'three parts natural calamity, seven parts man-made' to Liu Shaoqi, not Mao; note Mao's limited self-criticism and his withdrawal to the 'second line' while remaining Party Chairman (he had already handed the state chairmanship to Liu in April 1959).

Give grain output figures with a source and flag them as later-revised official statistics: approximately 200 million tonnes in 1958 (against wildly inflated claims of 375 million at the time), falling to about 170 million in 1959 and roughly 143-144 million in 1960, recovering only slowly in 1961 (State Statistical Bureau figures published in the 1980s, used by Western demographers).

Explain the causal mechanism rather than just listing policies: exaggerated reporting ('wind of exaggeration') led to procurement quotas set on fictional harvests, so the state took a rising share of a falling harvest (procurement around a quarter or more of output in 1959) while grain exports continued (several million tonnes in 1959-60); communal mess halls wasted stocks; labour was diverted to steel and irrigation; Lysenko-inspired techniques (close planting, deep ploughing) and the Four Pests campaign reduced yields.

Present the death-toll estimates as a contested range with named authors, not a single number: e.g. Frank Dikötter, Mao's Great Famine (2010), at least 45 million; Yang Jisheng, Tombstone (Chinese 2008, English 2012), about 36 million; Judith Banister (1987) and Basil Ashton et al. (1984) around 30 million; Jasper Becker, Hungry Ghosts (1996), about 30 million; Cao Shuji (2005) around 32.5 million; Peng Xizhe (1987) about 23 million; lower official-leaning Chinese estimates in the mid-teens of millions; and note that some Chinese scholars (e.g. Sun Jingxian) argue for far lower figures and that Cormac O Grada and others have criticised Dikotter's method - the answer must say estimates differ because of baseline mortality assumptions and whether lost births are counted.

Map the historiographical debate on responsibility with attribution: Dikötter (Mao personally, coercion and violence as central); Yang Jisheng (the totalitarian system and cadre terror); the CCP's own 1981 Resolution (leftist errors plus natural disasters, protecting the system); Amartya Sen's argument that famines of this scale do not occur where there is a free press and political opposition (information failure); Thomas Bernstein on excessive procurement; Justin Yifu Lin and Dennis Yang's 'exit rights' argument about communes; the role of provincial leaders such as Wu Zhipu in Henan (Xinyang) and Li Jingquan in Sichuan; and the weather/natural-disaster argument as a minor factor in most Western scholarship.

If it uses the alleged Mao remark from the March 1959 Shanghai meeting about letting 'half the people die', present it as disputed: Dikötter's reading versus critics who argue the remark concerned cutting industrial projects, not people, and that the context is contested.

Model the attribution phrasing the student asked for ('according to Dikötter...', 'Yang Jisheng argues...') and structure the answer as causes, consequences and debate so it can be turned into a 15-mark Paper 2 essay with a clear line of argument.

Explicitly flag which claims are settled (chronology, the Lushan purge, the fall in output) and which are contested (death toll, Mao's knowledge and intent, relative weight of weather), rather than giving one number as if settled.
pitfalls: Giving a single death toll (e.g. '45 million' or '30 million') as established fact without naming who estimates it and why estimates differ.

Misdating Lushan (it was 1959, not 1958 or 1960) or confusing Peng Dehuai with Lin Biao, Liu Shaoqi or Deng Xiaoping; saying Peng was executed (he was purged, later persecuted during the Cultural Revolution and died in 1974).
Attributing 'three parts natural disaster, seven parts man-made' to Mao or Zhou Enlai instead of Liu Shaoqi at the January-February 1962 cadres' conference.
Claiming Mao was removed from power in 1959 or 1962; he gave up the state chairmanship in April 1959 but remained Chairman of the Party.
Conflating the Great Leap Forward with the Hundred Flowers campaign (1956-57), the Anti-Rightist campaign of 1957 or the Cultural Revolution (1966-76).

Fabricating precise grain tonnages, procurement percentages, page numbers or verbatim quotations from historians; inventing historians or books; attributing Tombstone to Dikötter or Mao's Great Famine to Yang.
Quoting the 'half the people die' remark as proof of intent without noting that its interpretation is disputed.
Treating Dikötter's 45 million as the 'accepted' figure, or dismissing lower estimates without explaining the methodological disagreement.
Presenting the weather as the main cause (echoing the 1981 Party line) or ignoring it entirely, rather than weighing it against policy causes with attribution.
Giving a generic moral verdict ('Mao was evil') in place of a causal argument the student can use in a 15-mark essay.
